Mature River shiner (Notropis blennius) attain a maximum total length of 13.2 cm [Li = 13.2 cm], a value recorded from long-term survey collections across the Missouri River drainage. This species exhibits a relatively moderate ultimate size compared to other members of the genus Notropis, with most adults in breeding condition measuring between 8 and 11 cm. Analysis of growth increments from otoliths indicates that individuals approach this asymptotic length by their third or fourth year, with growth rates slowing considerably after the onset of sexual maturity. During routine electrofishing assessments, the largest specimen documented measured exactly 13.2 cm from the snout to the tip of the caudal fin, confirming earlier museum-based estimates. Regional variation in maximum size appears minimal across the species range, though populations in the northern periphery tend to average slightly smaller than those in the central Great Plains.

Puberty in this species is signaled by a total length of 5.9 cm [Lp = 5.9 cm], a measurement that corresponds to a standard length of 4.8 cm based on dissections of preserved specimens. Histological examination of gonad tissue from individuals collected during the pre-spawning period revealed that males and females first exhibit vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis, respectively, at this body size. The body mass of individuals at puberty averages approximately 1.67 g [Wwp = approximately 1.67 g], a figure derived from length-weight regressions applied to field-sampled fish. This weight at maturity is relatively modest, reflecting the species’ streamlined body form and its adaptation to swift-flowing lotic environments where energy is prioritized toward locomotion rather than somatic storage. Pubertal size is reached during the second summer of life in most populations, enabling young-of-the-year to participate in spawning events the following spring.

Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae of the River shiner emerge from demersal, adhesive eggs with an initial wet weight of approximately 0.00021 g [Wwb = approximately 0.00021 g], a figure based on the volumetric calculation from an average egg diameter of 0.9 mm. This minute birth mass places the species among the smaller-produced cyprinids, consistent with the production of numerous small eggs typical of pelagic-broadcast spawning fishes. The yolk-sac stage persists for roughly three to five days at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], during which the larva remains non-feeding and relies entirely on endogenous reserves. Following yolk resorption and mouth opening, the exotrophic transition begins, and juveniles rapidly gain mass as they shift to exogenous feeding on microcrustaceans and rotifers. The small size at hatching is correlated with high larval mortality, a pattern compensated by high fecundity in adult females.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], sexually mature females of 7.1 cm total length produce approximately 5.2 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 5.2 eggs per day]  when averaged over an annual reproductive cycle. At a slightly larger adult size of 9.1 cm total length, the daily reproductive output rises to approximately 8.2 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 8.2 eggs per day]  under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. These values were obtained from controlled spawning trials conducted over a full breeding season, during which individual females were isolated with males and their egg deposition recorded daily. The increase in reproductive output with body size is a common pattern among iteroparous cyprinids, reflecting greater abdominal volume and enhanced energetic capacity for vitellogenesis. The asymptotic body mass of adult River shiner, based on the length-weight relationship derived from extensive field sampling, reaches approximately 20.01 g [Wwi = approximately 20.01 g] for individuals attaining the maximum recorded total length. This value is consistent with the general scaling relationship observed in small-bodied cyprinids of the Great Plains, where body mass increases as approximately the cube of length. Specimens approaching this mass are typically robust, deep-bodied individuals in prime reproductive condition, often collected during the late spring spawning season when food resources are abundant and water temperatures are rising. Comparative analysis with congeneric species such as Notropis stramineus reveals that N. blennius attains a slightly greater ultimate mass, likely reflecting its occupation of larger, more productive river systems where prey availability is higher. The maximum longevity of 5 years [am = 5 years] is typical among small Notropis species, which rarely exceed six years in either wild or captive settings at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C].
